newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel approves Medicare budget plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel approves Medicare budget plan.

text.p: A House panel Wednesday unanimously approved a broad plan to restructure the Medicare program and cut spending by $115 billion over five years, as Democrats and Republicans closed ranks to support the measure.
The 13-0 vote by the House Ways and Means health subcommittee marks the first concrete action in Congress to translate a five-year balanced budget plan into law.

The bipartisan cooperation was in marked contrast to the bitter battles of two years ago when Democrats and Republicans were at war over possible changes in the popular health program for 38 million Americans.

"I'm not trying to battle, I'm trying to save, preserve and strengthen Medicare," said House Republican Rep. William Thomas, chairman of the subcommittee. He said the vote showed it was possible for Congress to make difficult policy changes.
The carefully crafted consensus bill avoids major increases in Medicare premiums, while expanding benefits and offering a wide array of health plan choices to recipients.

The bulk of the spending cuts would come from reducing Medicare payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers. The legislation provides new incentives to expand Medicare managed care to rural areas and allows doctors and hospitals to band together to form their own health networks.

The biggest skirmish during subcommittee debate came over a Republican proposal to allow up to 500,000 Medicare recipients to set up tax-free medical savings accounts. That plan is estimated to cost about $2 billion over five years.

Democrats offered an amendment to limit the pilot project to 100,000 special accounts, using the savings to start a new respite care program for families of Alzheimer's disease patients. The amendment was defeated on a party line vote.
"Give up 400,000 people who may never sign up (for MSAs) and then care for people trying to care for Alzheimer's patients," argued California Democratic Rep. Pete Stark.
The committee also turned back a Democratic amendment to eliminate a cap on non-economic awards in malpractice cases at $250,000. The White House opposes the malpractice plan.
The full Ways and Means Committee is expected to vote on the bill next week.

Under the MSA proposal, Medicare recipients would be given set payments to be deposited in a tax-free savings account. The account would be used in conjunction with catastrophic insurance policy with a deductible of no more than $6,000.
Funds could be withdrawn from the MSA for routine medical bills. Money left over could be rolled over to the next year.

Republicans say the proposal would make seniors more cost-conscious. The administration has feared the healthiest Medicare recipients would opt for MSAs -- leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular program and increasing costs.

While the budget deal is expected to keep Medicare solvent for a decade, both sides acknowledge major structural changes will be needed to protect the program in coming years as the baby boom generation reaches retirement age.
Other provisions of the Medicare plan include:
-- New consumer protections for managed care.

-- Freezing Medicare premiums at 25 percent of program costs, rather than letting them fall as allowed under current law. In addition, seniors would pay about $5.00 per month more. Premiums for Part B doctors' care would rise to $66.30 a month under the plan, compared to $61.50 under current law. The current premium is $42.50.
-- New payment controls for home health, skilled nursing and other fast-growing areas of Medicare.
-- A freeze on the hospital reimbursement rate next year.
-- New preventive services for Medicare recipients including mammograms, pap smears, prostate and colorectal cancer screening and diabetes benefits.
-- Tougher anti-fraud measures, including a proposal to cut providers out of the program after a third offense.
